title: The One With The Pediatrician

jokes.text: Wait a minute. Wait, you can't go to Tulsa. Maybe you forgot, but we have tickets to the Jets game next week!
jokes.setup: Everyone is reacting with genuine emotional concern about Chandler moving to Tulsa for a year.
jokes.punchline: Joey's urgent objection is entirely selfish — he's worried about missing a Jets game, not losing his friend.
jokes.explanation: Classic Joey selfishness used well here — the joke works because it's perfectly timed against genuine emotional stakes and the punchline is wholly character-specific. Joey's food/sports-over-friends priorities are his core comedic identity.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Do you have to go to Tulsa for work?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, I do. But I don't want to leave you.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: So don't go.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I have to. It's my job.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, what about us? What about this?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What about this stupid thing?

jokes.text: You can't go. I mean, you're the glue that holds this group together. / Really? / Not you.
jokes.setup: Ross says Chandler is 'the glue that holds the group together,' which Chandler takes as a sincere compliment.
jokes.punchline: Ross immediately clarifies he was talking to Monica, not Chandler — a brutal, deadpan deflation.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional economy — the entire joke lives in two words: 'Not you.' The misdirection is clean, the deflation is brutal, and the beat of Chandler's hopeful 'Really?' makes the puncture land harder. One of the episode's tightest constructions.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, nothing says 'I'm behind you 100 percent' like calling our marriage 'this stupid thing.'

jokes.text: I call their apartment!
jokes.setup: Everyone is processing the emotional news that Chandler and Monica are moving away.
jokes.punchline: Joey's immediate instinct is to claim dibs on their Manhattan apartment, cutting through any emotional gravity.
jokes.explanation: Another sharp Joey moment landing seconds after his Jets joke — the rapid-fire selfish responses create an escalating pattern. The brevity and immediacy of 'I call their apartment!' is perfectly Joey.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: The Jets game? The Jets game?! Chandler, how could you miss the Jets game?

jokes.text: A person named 'Wiener.' God, that kills me.
jokes.setup: Joey and Monica are having a sincere conversation about growing up and maturity.
jokes.punchline: Joey's train of thought derails entirely — he's still stuck on the funny name.
jokes.explanation: It's a low-brow joke elevated by its timing — Joey delivers it in the middle of an earnest maturity conversation, which makes his immaturity funnier. The name itself isn't clever, but Joey's inability to move past it is character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You're the glue holding this group together.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Really? Me?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: No, I'm talking to someone else.

jokes.text: I'd like to meet a nice, mature, commitment-minded lady. And looks aren't as important as... Nah, she's gotta be hot.
jokes.setup: Joey sincerely claims he's ready for a mature relationship and that looks aren't as important anymore.
jokes.punchline: He immediately abandons the pretense — 'Nah, she's gotta be hot.'
jokes.explanation: The brief pause before 'Nah' is key — Joey almost convinces himself before reverting. Perfectly character-specific and efficiently structured. The self-awareness makes it slightly more than a cheap gag.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. So you're moving out? Both of you?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yes, we found a place in the suburbs.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh my God. Oh my God! When are you leaving?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Next month.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Next month?! I call the apartment!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Joey, you can't just call it.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Why not? I called it! I'm moving in! I get the bedroom, the living room, the kitchen—

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Joey, there's a lease. There's an application process.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: An application? Monica, I've been your neighbor for ten years. What do you need, references?

jokes.text: Sandy Poopack. / 'Poopack'?
jokes.setup: Monica is trying to find a blind date for Joey and thinks of a good candidate.
jokes.punchline: The name 'Poopack' — Joey's horrified one-word reaction is the entire joke.
jokes.explanation: A cheap funny-name joke, but the rhythm is good — Monica says it straight, Joey repeats it in disbelief. Quick and functional. Not much craft, but the economy is there.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Can I have caffeine while breastfeeding?

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.line: Of course. I'm Dr. Wiener.

jokes.text: All right. Well, that rules out Lana Titwyler.
jokes.setup: Joey rejected Sandy Poopack for having a funny name.
jokes.punchline: Monica immediately produces another candidate with an even more ridiculous name, Lana Titwyler, acknowledging this rules her out too.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'Poopack' to 'Titwyler' is the joke — Monica's deadpan delivery of the callback makes it funnier than the original. The structure of immediately discarding the second name is tight.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Rachel, you call the doctor for every little thing.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, I like to be informed.

jokes.text: I won't live in a different state than you for 208 days out of the year. / That's fast math. We could use you in Tulsa.
jokes.setup: Monica emotionally declares she won't be separated from Chandler for 208 days a year.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's response ignores the emotional content entirely and compliments her speed arithmetic, then recruits her for Tulsa.
jokes.explanation: Chandler's deflecting-with-absurdity is his signature move, and 'We could use you in Tulsa' is a satisfying non-sequitur that undercuts the emotional moment without being mean. Character-specific and well-structured.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You don't need to call the doctor.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Hi, yes, I'd like to make an appointment.

jokes.text: You said that without gagging. / I know!
jokes.setup: Monica sincerely says she'll follow Chandler to Tulsa because he's her husband.
jokes.punchline: Chandler notes — with surprise — that she said it without gagging, which Monica also celebrates, suggesting 'going to Tulsa' is so unappealing it normally provokes a physical reaction.
jokes.explanation: The mutual acknowledgment that agreeing to Tulsa is a physical ordeal is a sweet-and-funny beat. Monica's 'I know!' is an endearing confession. Good economy and character work.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Dr. Noonan? NOONAN?! That's the best name I've ever heard! I'm gonna request him for everything. Colonoscopy? I want Noonan. Root canal? Noonan. I don't even care what he does, I just wanna say, 'Thanks, Noonan!'

jokes.text: Who the hell was that? / Dr. Wiener.
jokes.setup: Ross is woken at 3 AM by Rachel shouting angrily on the phone.
jokes.punchline: It's Dr. Wiener — the pediatrician they've been over-calling — having apparently snapped back at Rachel.
jokes.explanation: The reveal lands clean — 'Dr. Wiener' as a two-word punchline is perfectly economical, and 'Up yours too!' from Rachel implies the doctor finally lost patience. The escalation of the running Dr. Wiener gag pays off well.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm ready for a serious relationship where looks don't matter.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: She just has to be really, really hot.

jokes.text: Rach, you can't call people at 3:00 in the morning. / You know what? You sound just like his wife.
jokes.setup: Ross scolds Rachel for calling the doctor at 3 AM.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's comeback reveals that Dr. Wiener's wife also scolded her — meaning this has happened enough for her to earn comparison to the doctor's angry spouse.
jokes.explanation: Implies the problem is worse than we knew — this has gone so far that the doctor's wife now gets involved. Good layering on the running gag.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Sandy Poopak? Hehehehe.

jokes.text: What was it? / Hiccups.
jokes.setup: Ross presses Rachel to confess what was actually wrong with Emma that justified the 3 AM call.
jokes.punchline: Hiccups. The catastrophic urgency was for hiccups.
jokes.explanation: The one-word answer 'Hiccups' is the entire joke. Classic bathos — maximum anxiety for minimum cause. Well-timed beat.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh yeah? Well I know a guy named Bidet Tron.

jokes.text: Well, not anymore I can't. He fired us!
jokes.setup: Ross tells Rachel she can't keep calling Dr. Wiener for every little thing.
jokes.punchline: The option is moot — Dr. Wiener has fired them as patients.
jokes.explanation: The escalation lands — getting fired by your pediatrician is a perfect absurd consequence, and 'He fired us' has a great rhythm. Strong payoff to the running gag.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You'll be okay while I'm gone for four days, right?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Monica, I haven't even finished the question.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh. Sorry. No.

jokes.text: I think he's dead. / Why does everything happen to me?
jokes.setup: Rachel suggests seeing Ross's childhood pediatrician, Dr. Gettleman. Ross says he thinks the doctor is dead.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's response is a melodramatic self-pity spiral — reacting to a stranger's possible death purely as a personal inconvenience.
jokes.explanation: Classic Rachel self-centeredness — mourning the inconvenience of a stranger's death. Character-specific and efficiently delivered.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: 208 days out of the year.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Wow, someone's been doing their math.

jokes.text: You're not feeling well? What do you have? Rubella? Because don't go near Emma, she has not had that shot.
jokes.setup: Ross mentions he's not feeling well as a reason to go to bed.
jokes.punchline: Rachel immediately leaps to 'Rubella' — a dramatic over-diagnosis that pivots from concern for Ross to concern for Emma.
jokes.explanation: The diagnostic leap to Rubella is funny, but the second half — pivoting to worry about Emma rather than Ross — is the sharper beat. Shows Rachel's anxious new-parent brain.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'll go to Tulsa with you.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yeah. This is growth for me. I usually hate change.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I know.

jokes.text: You know, come to think of it, it does feel rubella-like.
jokes.setup: Rachel has dramatically suggested Ross has Rubella.
jokes.punchline: Ross, playing along sarcastically, confirms that it does 'feel rubella-like' — a deadpan capitulation to her hypochondria.
jokes.explanation: The phrase 'rubella-like' is the joke — it sounds medical and specific while being completely meaningless. Ross's dry delivery elevates it.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: No, no, no, that is not what the book says! Yes, I have the book. No, I don't care what you went to school for!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, maybe your school was wrong! Have you thought about that?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You know what, I'm gonna get a second opinion. Actually, I'm gonna get a third opinion because I don't trust you!

jokes.text: Wiener! Wiener! Wiener! / Rachel! / Great! Now he's gonna know it was me!
jokes.setup: It's 3 AM, the Dr. Wiener conflict has just been established.
jokes.punchline: Rachel begins shouting 'Wiener!' repeatedly down the street (or out the window), apparently at the doctor. Ross's alarm is answered by Rachel's completely illogical fear of being identified — as if the doctor won't already know.
jokes.explanation: The best payoff in the Dr. Wiener arc — Rachel shouting the name and then worrying about anonymity is perfectly absurd logic. 'Now he's gonna know it was me!' is the standout line, a beautiful piece of Rachel irrationality. The audience has been primed by multiple escalating beats.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Who were you just arguing with?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: My baby's pediatrician.

jokes.text: I can't tell you how I know this, but she is not opposed to threesomes.
jokes.setup: Monica is describing Mary Ellen as a great match for Joey — smart, cute, funny.
jokes.punchline: She adds this specific piece of intel while deliberately withholding the source, which is funnier than any explanation could be.
jokes.explanation: The 'I can't tell you how I know this' framing is funnier than the revelation itself — it implies Monica has a whole backstory she's suppressing. The economy of leaving that mystery intact is excellent craft. Joey's simple 'All right' response lands perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Rachel, you called the doctor at 3 in the morning?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, I was worried!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: It's 3 AM! That's completely inconsiderate.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh please. His wife called me this morning and said the same thing.

jokes.text: What's his last name? / Damn it! Is there no mystery left in romance anymore?!
jokes.setup: Phoebe asks for more details about her blind date, specifically his last name.
jokes.punchline: Monica snaps — she made up a name on the spot and hasn't thought past 'Mike.' Her outburst about 'mystery in romance' is a cover for her own failure.
jokes.explanation: The deflection into philosophy of romance is a fun non-sequitur, and the audience knows why Monica is panicking. The comedic irony of hiding incompetence behind romantic idealism is well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What was wrong with Emma that required a 3am call?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: It was just hiccups.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Just hiccups? Do you know what time it is?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, they were really bad hiccups!

jokes.text: Why'd I have to say Mike? I don't know a Mike! Why couldn't I have said...? / There's no guys in there!
jokes.setup: Monica realizes she invented a blind date named Mike and has no one to set Phoebe up with.
jokes.punchline: She desperately checks her address book (or contacts) for a 'Mike' and finds none. 'There's no guys in there!' implies the visual of her frantically flipping through contacts.
jokes.explanation: Monica's panic spiral is funny but slightly over-played. 'There's no guys in there!' is the best line — implies something funny about Monica's social circle. Good energy, moderate craft.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You can't keep calling the doctor for every little thing.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What? I have a legitimate concern!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Rachel, you called him yesterday because you thought you had a hangnail.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: It could have been serious!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, it got serious. The doctor fired us as patients.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: He what?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yeah, he said we're his most high-maintenance patients ever. He actually used the word 'escalated.'

jokes.text: It's impossible to find a good doctor. How do you know the good ones from the ones who'll push their penis against your knee?
jokes.setup: Rachel and Monica are discussing finding a new pediatrician.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's criteria for a 'bad' doctor is shockingly specific — a doctor who pushes his penis against your knee — implying a very particular past experience.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'penis against your knee' is what makes it — a generalized bad doctor concern becomes hyper-specific, implying a real incident. Monica's 'I know what she's talking about' follow-up raises the stakes further and is an equal laugh. Surprising for Friends.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Actually, I think I might have measles too. And possibly mumps. Oh, and I'm pretty sure my spleen just fell out.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm kidding! I'm just messing with you.

jokes.text: Excuse me? / I know what she's talking about.
jokes.setup: Rachel has just said something shocking about a doctor who pushes his penis against your knee.
jokes.punchline: Ross's scandalized 'Excuse me?' is immediately followed by Monica confirming she's also had this experience — escalating the horror.
jokes.explanation: Monica's quiet 'I know what she's talking about' is devastatingly funny — it validates Rachel AND implies a shared history between the two women with a terrible doctor. Ross's 'Excuse me?' straight-man beat sets it up perfectly. The two-beat structure is clean.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Wiener! Wiener!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Rachel!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh no.

jokes.text: He used to have a recurring nightmare. It freaked him out. / What was it? / That I was going to eat him.
jokes.setup: Monica reveals that Ross saw a childhood therapist, and Rachel asks what his nightmare was about.
jokes.punchline: Monica: 'That I was going to eat him.' Delivered flat, as if this is totally reasonable information to share.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The setup is a layered mystery (therapist for a nightmare) that invites imaginative speculation, then Monica's flat, matter-of-fact delivery of 'That I was going to eat him' is perfectly calibrated. It's character-specific (sibling cruelty toward Ross is a series staple), economical (four words), and deeply quotable. Monica's total lack of guilt or self-reflection makes it funnier still. Earns its 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Phoebe, what are you wearing?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: What? I think I look great!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You look like you got dressed in the dark at a thrift store.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, I'm sorry, I didn't realize we were going for 'Joey's idea of fashion,' which is basically just whatever makes you look like you're trying too hard.

jokes.text: How do Joey and I know each other? If I had a nickel for every time somebody's asked me that.
jokes.setup: Mary Ellen asks how Joey and Mike know each other — a totally natural question given they're supposed to be old friends.
jokes.punchline: Mike (a complete stranger recruited off the street) plays along by implying this is a question he gets constantly — an absurd claim that acknowledges the fiction's ridiculousness.
jokes.explanation: Mike's confidence in a situation where he has zero information is funny — he sounds like someone who truly has a long history with Joey while knowing nothing. The idiom 'If I had a nickel' creates an air of weary nostalgia that's completely unearned and therefore perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Mary Ellen was my best friend in high school. She was beautiful, smart, kind to animals... and a raging nymphomaniac.

jokes.text: From school. / We met in college. / I mean high school.
jokes.setup: Mike and Joey are attempting to establish their fake friendship history.
jokes.punchline: They contradict each other immediately — Mike says school, Joey says college, then corrects to high school.
jokes.explanation: Classic cringe comedy — the cover story falls apart in real time. The escalating correction (school > college > high school) shows Joey's desperation. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What's your last name?

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: Hannigan.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, Mike Hannigan. No! No, that ruins it! It was so much better when he was just Mike. Now he's a guy with a last name. He's a guy with a job, probably a social security number. It's too real, it's too much!

jokes.text: Well, I'm a lawyer. / Mike, attorney at law!
jokes.setup: Mike improvises that he's a lawyer to give himself credibility in the fake backstory.
jokes.punchline: Joey immediately announces it like a business card — 'Mike, attorney at law!' — far too enthusiastically for a casual conversation, blowing their cover further.
jokes.explanation: Joey's over-enthusiasm undercuts the lie — a good bit of cringe. The 'attorney at law' formal suffix is the touch that makes it funny.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh no, oh no, oh no. I promised Joey a date with Mike and I don't know any Mikes!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Okay, let me look through my purse, maybe I have a Mike in here.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I've got a Brian, a David, a couple of Jons... no Mike.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I've got a harmonica, some gum, a half-eaten sandwich... still no Mike!

jokes.text: Actually, I just gave up my practice. / What? / That's the kind of thing you usually run by me.
jokes.setup: Joey has just established Mike as a lawyer.
jokes.punchline: Mike immediately contradicts it by saying he quit, and Joey's indignant 'That's the kind of thing you usually run by me' plays perfectly as if they have a real friendship with established protocols.
jokes.explanation: Joey's 'That's the kind of thing you usually run by me' is the standout line in the double-date sequence. It's brilliant because Joey commits fully to the fiction in precisely the wrong direction — his outrage is real, as if Mike has violated a genuine friendship agreement. The irony that Joey literally just met this man makes it land hard. Well above average craft.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: How do you find a good doctor?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, you could try asking around.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I tried that. My last doctor told me to lose weight, and then he asked me out.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: That's horrible!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I know. And he had such good hands too.

jokes.text: Great. I like that better than the lawyer thing. / Which is why I waited until now to introduce you to Mike. / You thought he was still a lawyer.
jokes.setup: Mike reveals he gave up law to pursue piano. Phoebe says she likes that better.
jokes.punchline: Joey retroactively reframes withholding Mike's identity as a strategic reveal — 'Which is why I waited' — as if he planned all of this. Phoebe immediately punctures the lie.
jokes.explanation: Joey's attempt to rewrite history is funny but Phoebe's instant deflation of it is the better beat. Good exchange rhythm.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Can you believe my doctor kept hitting on me during my exam?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, mine too. But then I realized he was just checking my prostate.

jokes.text: Slim Pickins. / Nothing, huh? / No. Slim Pickins. It's a barbecue joint.
jokes.setup: Chandler says he's found slim pickings for restaurant jobs in Tulsa. Monica thinks he means the idiom.
jokes.punchline: It's literally a restaurant called Slim Pickins — a barbecue joint.
jokes.explanation: A clean double-meaning joke with excellent structure — Monica's misreading is totally natural, and the reveal of the literal restaurant name is satisfying. The 'Nothing, huh? / No. Slim Pickins.' exchange is paced perfectly. Good craft.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I saw Dr. Gettleman's daughter the other day, and she said he was fine.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, his daughter's face says otherwise.

jokes.text: They're looking for somebody to shovel mesquite.
jokes.setup: Chandler says the job listing is for a 'cook' — which is a stretch — at Slim Pickins
jokes.punchline: The actual job is to shovel mesquite — glorified manual labor presented as a culinary opportunity for Monica
jokes.explanation: Good extension of the previous joke. The deflation of 'cook' to 'mesquite shoveler' is both funny and illustrates the stark career options Monica faces in Tulsa. Chandler's deadpan delivery of terrible news is well-suited to his character.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: He had a recurring nightmare about me eating him.

jokes.text: 'Slim Pickins'? That is so cheesy. / Well, So Cheesy also has an opening.
jokes.setup: Monica calls the restaurant name 'so cheesy.'
jokes.punchline: Chandler reveals 'So Cheesy' is also an actual restaurant with a job opening — same wordplay trick doubled.
jokes.explanation: The escalation of the same wordplay trick in rapid succession — 'So Cheesy also has an opening' — is funnier than the original because the audience is now primed for it. The speed and economy are exceptional, and the callback structure is tight. 'Whole Hog?' continuing the gag immediately after is further escalation. This sequence is among the episode's best-constructed comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Mike!

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: Oh, uh... hi? Do I know you?

jokes.text: Whole Hog? / It's gonna be tough to keep kosher in Tulsa.
jokes.setup: The running gag of Tulsa restaurant names continues with 'Whole Hog.'
jokes.punchline: Chandler's observation about keeping kosher lands both as an endpoint to the restaurant-name gag and as a cultural joke.
jokes.explanation: A solid button on the restaurant-name escalation — Chandler steps outside the naming game to deliver a genuine observation. Slightly weaker than the previous two beats but serves as a good landing point.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Okay, so you're pretending to be Mike. Really commit to it. Make me believe you're Mike.

dialogue.speaker: Stranger
dialogue.line: But I actually am Mike.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, that's amazing! You're so good at this!

jokes.text: Would you like a lollipop? / Do you even have to ask?
jokes.setup: Dr. Gettleman finishes examining what appears to be a child patient and offers a lollipop.
jokes.punchline: Ross — an adult — eagerly accepts with 'Do you even have to ask?' implying he still sees this pediatrician for himself.
jokes.explanation: The reveal of Ross still seeing his pediatrician is the episode's best-sustained joke, and 'Do you even have to ask?' is the first brick in that wall. Ross's eagerness for the lollipop is perfectly childlike. The setup through Rachel being there to bring Emma lets this land as a shock.

dialogue.speaker: Mary Ellen
dialogue.line: How do you two know each other?

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: You know, it's a long story.

jokes.text: He is alive!
jokes.setup: Ross said Dr. Gettleman was dead. Rachel has just walked into the pediatrician's office and seen him.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's stunned 'He is alive!' is a callback to Ross's misinformation, delivered as though she's witnessing a miracle.
jokes.explanation: The dramatic delivery of 'He is alive!' is funnier than the revelation itself — Rachel treats this as a resurrection. Quick and clean callback.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: We met in college.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: High school.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Right, high school. We were roommates.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: We lived three states apart.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, we visited each other every weekend.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: I've never left New Jersey.

jokes.text: Mike hit my mom with a car. / No, I didn't. / That's okay. I have forgiven you.
jokes.setup: Mary Ellen is questioning how Joey and Mike could be old friends given she's never heard of Mike.
jokes.punchline: Joey explains they had a 'falling out' because Mike hit his mom with a car — a wildly escalated explanation. Mike denies it; Joey graciously forgives him anyway.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Joey's escalation to 'Mike hit my mom with a car' is a perfect absurdist improvisation, and the exchange that follows — Mike denying it, Joey forgiving him anyway — is brilliantly structured. Joey's magnanimity in forgiving something that never happened is the topper. The three-beat structure (accusation / denial / forgiveness) is tight and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: I'm a lawyer.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: A lawyer? And you didn't think to call me? We go way back!

jokes.text: Is your mom okay? / Please, we're trying to have a conversation.
jokes.setup: Mary Ellen, reasonably, asks if Joey's mom is okay after the car incident.
jokes.punchline: Joey dismisses her concern as an interruption — a stunning display of rudeness that reveals he cares more about maintaining the lie than his fictional mother's welfare.
jokes.explanation: Joey's breezy 'Please, we're trying to have a conversation' in response to concern for his fictionally injured mother is a great character beat. The callousness reads as oblivious rather than mean, which keeps Joey likeable.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What? It's a real restaurant!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I know, but you have to admit, it's a pretty accurate description of the job market right now.

jokes.text: You're a lot nicer on 'Days of Our Lives.' / 'Days of Our Lives'! That's why you look so familiar!
jokes.setup: Mary Ellen recognizes Joey from his soap opera work.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's revelation — that she now recognizes 'Mike' because she knows Joey from TV — exposes that she's been sitting across from a stranger the whole time.
jokes.explanation: The reveal lands cleanly — Phoebe realizing she doesn't actually know her date is a good cringe escalation. 'That's why you look so familiar!' is delivered with Phoebe's signature guileless enthusiasm which makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: 'Cook' may be a stretch for this job. The actual job is just shoveling wood chips.

jokes.text: Of course we do. He's playing a game we used to play in high school. We pretend we don't know each other.
jokes.setup: Phoebe has just realized she doesn't know Mike, blowing up Joey's setup.
jokes.punchline: Joey improvises that 'pretending not to know each other' is a game they played — an absurdist retcon that's entirely implausible.
jokes.explanation: Joey's desperate improvisation is funny but slightly weaker than the car/mom joke. The game invention is implausible enough to get a laugh but not quite absurdist enough to be great.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That name is so cheesy.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Actually, there's a restaurant down the street literally called 'So Cheesy.'

jokes.text: You remember that one where I punch you in the face for not being cool?
jokes.setup: Joey is trying to sell the idea that he and Mike play games together, including pretending not to know each other.
jokes.punchline: He threatens Mike with a fake 'game' of punching him in the face for 'not being cool' — a transparently coercive threat disguised as nostalgia.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The framing of a violent threat as a nostalgic 'game' is brilliantly absurdist, and 'for not being cool' as the stated trigger is delightful. The specificity of the condition (not being cool) elevates it above a generic threat. Character-specific to Joey's desperate-but-amiable improvisation style.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh! What about 'The Place Where We Make Pasta'?

jokes.text: Let me ask you something: How many sisters does Joey have? / Six. / What are you doing? I said seven!
jokes.setup: Mary Ellen tests whether Mike and Joey really know each other by asking how many sisters Joey has.
jokes.punchline: Mike guesses six; Joey corrects him to seven, which also reveals he has seven sisters — a real fact that Mike got wrong.
jokes.explanation: Joey's indignant 'What are you doing? I said seven!' is priceless — he's angry about Mike failing a test of a friendship that doesn't exist. The structure is clean: test, wrong answer, genuine outrage. Joey's investment in the lie being done correctly is both absurd and character-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, this is great. A steakhouse, a barbecue place, and a Brazilian churrascaria. You know what? I'm keeping kosher.

jokes.text: Joey, why did you set me up with a stranger? / Because I forgot about our date. I'm so sorry.
jokes.setup: Phoebe confronts Joey about the deception.
jokes.punchline: Joey's reason: he simply forgot. No elaborate excuse, no cover story — just pure Joey honesty about his own failure.
jokes.explanation: The deflation of all the elaborate deception into 'I forgot' is very Joey. The honesty of the admission undercuts any further argument. Character-specific and efficiently delivered.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yes! Yes, absolutely! When do I start?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa! Monica, what about Tulsa?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What? Oh, right. Tulsa. Um... I'm not going to Tulsa.

jokes.text: You are unbelievable. I spent so much time finding the perfect girl for you. Mary Ellen is really smart and cute and loose.
jokes.setup: Phoebe is angrily listing Mary Ellen's virtues to emphasize what Joey squandered.
jokes.punchline: The list goes: smart, cute, and... 'loose' — presumably Phoebe using the wrong word (perhaps meaning 'easygoing' or mirroring Monica's 'not opposed to threesomes' intel in her own Phoebe-filtered way).
jokes.explanation: Phoebe using 'loose' either innocently or knowingly is a great character beat — either she doesn't realize the connotation (classic Phoebe obliviousness) or she does and is making a point. Both readings are funny. The word landing in an angry list of compliments is well-timed.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Wait a minute... you're alive?

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Gettleman
dialogue.line: Of course I'm alive.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God. Ross lied to me!

jokes.text: I'm out of here. / It was nice meeting you. / You're leaving too? / I'll stay if you can tell me my name.
jokes.setup: The double date has collapsed. Mary Ellen storms out. Mike begins to leave too.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe asks Mike to stay; he offers a condition — she has to tell him his name, which she doesn't know, since he's a stranger.
jokes.explanation: 'I'll stay if you can tell me my name' is a lovely exit line — it's both a joke and a romantic setup (she can't, so he goes). The economy is excellent and the character has established enough wit to make this feel natural.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Gettleman
dialogue.line: Would you like a lollipop?

dialogue.speaker: Adult Patient
dialogue.line: Yes, please!

jokes.text: It's just a little outside of Tulsa. / How far outside? / Manhattan?
jokes.setup: Monica describes a job opportunity as 'just a little outside of Tulsa,' using classic understatement.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's guessed 'Manhattan?' lands as both obvious and funny — the reveal that Monica considers a 1,500-mile distance 'a little outside.'
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — the entire joke is Monica's euphemism and Chandler's one-word guess, 'Manhattan?' The question mark is crucial; Chandler already knows but asks to let Monica hear herself. Clean, well-structured, and quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: We had a huge falling out. Mike said something to me that I just... I couldn't get past it.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: He said my haircut made me look like a lesbian.

jokes.text: I'm gonna miss this hand!
jokes.setup: Chandler is processing the possibility that Monica might stay in New York while he goes to Tulsa.
jokes.punchline: His expression of what he'll miss is specifically 'this hand' — a randomly specific, oddly intimate thing to mourn. It implies he's holding or looking at Monica's hand.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'this hand' is disarmingly sweet and funny simultaneously. It's an absurd synecdoche — he means her whole person but can only articulate the hand he's holding. Classic Chandler: comedy used to access genuine emotion.

dialogue.speaker: Mary Ellen
dialogue.line: Is your mom okay? She got hit by a car!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, she's fine. But you're interrupting my story!

jokes.text: I see you Monday before you go to work, and Thursday when you get back, and I always work late on Tuesdays, so really if you think about it, it's really just one day.
jokes.setup: Monica is trying to convince Chandler that four days apart isn't that bad.
jokes.punchline: Through increasingly creative arithmetic, Monica reduces four days to 'really just one day' — the same speed-math energy she showed earlier, now used for rationalization.
jokes.explanation: Monica's math abilities as a character trait get a second use here, and it's a nice callback. The logic is hilariously tortured ('I work late Tuesdays, so...') and the conclusion — 'just one day' — is delivered with complete sincerity.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: He didn't recognize me! We went to high school together!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh, you know what? I'm gonna find him and I'm gonna play a little game with him. It's called 'Remember when we used to do this?' And then I punch him in the face.

jokes.text: I know it must be important to you when you start chattering like a monkey.
jokes.setup: Chandler is telling Monica he thinks she should take the job.
jokes.punchline: His signal that Monica's desires are sincere is when she 'chatters like a monkey' — a bizarrely specific but affectionate observation about her personality.
jokes.explanation: Specific, character-grounded, and affectionate — Chandler has observed this behavior long enough to have a name for it. 'Chattering like a monkey' is vivid and specific enough to suggest real truth. Monica's 'That's the nicest thing anybody's ever said to me' response makes it a sweet moment that earns the laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Mary Ellen
dialogue.line: How many sisters does Joey have?

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: Seven.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I have nine sisters.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: Nine! That's what I said.

jokes.text: That's the nicest thing anybody's ever said to me.
jokes.setup: Chandler has just compared Monica to a chattering monkey as a compliment.
jokes.punchline: Monica receives this as the most touching thing she's ever heard — which, combined with the content of the compliment, is funny.
jokes.explanation: Works as the button to Chandler's monkey line. Monica's earnestness makes the absurd compliment land as genuinely sweet, which is a tonal tightrope the show walks well.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: I did not hit your mother with a car.

jokes.text: Ross still sees his pediatrician!
jokes.setup: Rachel has been asked to keep a secret about their pediatrician visit. She promised.
jokes.punchline: She immediately announces it the moment they walk in the door.
jokes.explanation: Classic promise-then-immediate-betrayal structure — a reliable sitcom setup executed efficiently. 'You promised not to say anything / I know. / Ross still sees his pediatrician!' has great comedic rhythm. The fact that she acknowledges breaking the promise while breaking it is the extra beat that elevates it.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You're smart, you're funny, you're kind, you're generous...

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: And you're a little loose.

dialogue.speaker: Mary Ellen
dialogue.line: I am not loose!

jokes.text: He is a brilliant diagnostician! / Diagnostician or boo-boo fixer?
jokes.setup: Ross defends seeing his pediatrician by calling Dr. Gettleman a 'brilliant diagnostician.'
jokes.punchline: Monica reduces the clinical term with 'boo-boo fixer' — the pediatric equivalent.
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of Ross's clinical vocabulary against Monica's childlike 'boo-boo fixer' is a clean, well-executed bit. Good economy and sibling dynamic.

dialogue.speaker: Mary Ellen
dialogue.line: Okay, you know what? I'm leaving.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. I can prove I know things about you.

dialogue.speaker: Mary Ellen
dialogue.line: Oh yeah? Name one thing.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You're... a woman.

jokes.text: Every time I go in there, he makes a big deal. 'Look, it's my favorite patient.' / Does he say that before he sticks his thermometer in your tushy?
jokes.setup: Ross is rhapsodizing about how Dr. Gettleman treats him as a special patient.
jokes.punchline: Monica asks if the 'favorite patient' treatment comes before the rectal thermometer — a callback to the fact that Ross is an adult in a pediatric office.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best-constructed jokes. 'Tushy' doing heavy lifting as a child-vocabulary word used in an adult context is perfect. The implication that Ross gets a rectal thermometer as an adult is both horrifying and hilarious. Monica's delivery would be flat, matter-of-fact sibling cruelty at its finest. Strong character integration and structure.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: It's a little outside Tulsa.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: How far outside?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Manhattan.

jokes.text: I seem to remember someone bringing his security blanket to college. / That was not a security blanket. That was a wall hanging. / It didn't spend much time on the wall!
jokes.setup: Ross tries to deflect Monica's teasing by pointing out her own childhood attachment issues (security blanket).
jokes.punchline: Monica's retort — 'It didn't spend much time on the wall!' — confirms the blanket's real purpose while undercutting Ross's reframing.
jokes.explanation: The three-beat structure is tight: accusation, defensive reframing, devastating rejoinder. 'It didn't spend much time on the wall!' is a great topper — Monica both confirms the original joke and wins the exchange. Pure sibling comedy with strong character grounding.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh, I'm gonna miss this.

jokes.text: I'm sorry, really. I'm a pretty nice guy. Just ask my parole officer.
jokes.setup: Mike is apologizing to Phoebe for going along with Joey's deception.
jokes.punchline: He vouches for his character by suggesting she ask his parole officer — which raises more questions than it answers.
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection — the character reference that undermines the character reference. 'Parole officer' as a punchline to 'I'm a nice guy' is a reliable structure executed crisply. Mike's self-awareness about landing badly ('Apparently, I'm not a funny guy') is a nice meta follow-up.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: So really, when you think about it, one day apart is basically the same as four days apart.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yes, that's exactly how math works.

jokes.text: Apparently, I'm not a funny guy.
jokes.setup: Mike's parole officer joke has not landed with Phoebe.
jokes.punchline: Mike acknowledges the failed joke by deadpanning that he's apparently not funny — which is itself funnier than the original joke.
jokes.explanation: The meta acknowledgment of a failed joke is a smart move that characterizes Mike as self-aware and appealing. Efficiently delivered.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: A monkey? That's so cute! Monkeys are adorable!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Monica, that's not—

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'm going to start doing that more often. Thank you!

jokes.text: Because I was told that I'd get a free dinner, which I didn't. And that I'd meet a pretty girl, which I did.
jokes.setup: Phoebe asks why Mike went along with the whole scheme.
jokes.punchline: He accounts for both promises — the dinner failed, the pretty girl succeeded — delivered with parallel structure and a compliment landing as the second beat.
jokes.explanation: The two-part parallel structure — failure / success — is well-constructed, and the compliment landing as the second beat is an effective romantic setup. The beat that follows (Phoebe's reaction) would be a good visual.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, oh my God! You will not believe what I just found out about Ross!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: He's in love with Rachel!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: We know.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, Monica, we've known for like, years.

jokes.text: That wouldn't stand in the way of a true pianist.
jokes.setup: Mike says he can't prove his piano skills because there's no piano in the bar.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe invokes the concept of a 'true pianist' who doesn't need a piano — an absurd and romantic standard that Mike then meets by air-playing convincingly.
jokes.explanation: Very Phoebe — she invents a philosophical standard for musical authenticity that is completely made up. The humor is in her earnestness and the fact that Mike actually goes along with it.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: He's a brilliant diagnostician!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, he's a pediatrician, Ross. He just looks at kids and goes, 'Yep, that's a kid.'

jokes.text: But right now I'm working on a couple Iron Maiden covers.
jokes.setup: Phoebe describes her musical style as 'acoustic, folksy stuff' — in line with her known character.
jokes.punchline: She's apparently also working on Iron Maiden covers — a jarring non-sequitur that plays against her gentle musical image.
jokes.explanation: Perfect character non-sequitur — Phoebe's folk/acoustic image is immediately upended by Iron Maiden, delivered as though this is completely consistent. The specificity of the band name (not generic 'metal' but Iron Maiden) is crucial to the joke's quality. Very high character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, and I'm sure you're his favorite patient. Right up until he has to give you a rectal exam and realizes you're just like all the other guys.

jokes.text: Excuse me. I don't mean to be a jerk, but the baby with the rash came in after me.
jokes.setup: Ross is in the pediatrician's waiting room, ostensibly there to meet Rachel.
jokes.punchline: Ross is complaining about waiting room order — competing with actual sick children for appointment priority at a pediatrician's office he attends as an adult patient.
jokes.explanation: Ross asserting his appointment rights over a baby with a rash is a beautiful comedic image. 'The baby with the rash came in after me' as a complaint is absurd and character-perfect — Ross's oblivious self-seriousness in a children's medical setting is perfectly executed.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: It's a wall hanging! It's a Navajo weaving!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Really? Because there's still a tag on it that says 'Blanket'.

jokes.text: Look at this! My two best friends!
jokes.setup: Phoebe and Mike are having a genuinely romantic moment; Joey suddenly appears
jokes.punchline: Joey calls Mike his 'best friend' despite having met him an hour ago under false pretenses — either he's oblivious or charitably adopting Mike
jokes.explanation: Quick character beat — Joey has fully absorbed Mike into his social world despite the disaster. 'My two best friends!' is funny in context because one of them he met hours ago. Functional rather than exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: I'm a good person, Mary Ellen. I have a parole officer who can vouch for me.

jokes.text: Mommy, I can't find Waldo. / What, the circus? He's behind the elephant.
jokes.setup: A child in the waiting room can't find Waldo in a Where's Waldo book.
jokes.punchline: Ross immediately answers — he knows the specific Waldo location in the circus book without looking, demonstrating that he has memorized children's puzzle books, entirely consistent with being a pediatric patient as an adult.
jokes.explanation: The fact that Ross knows this answer confirms how often he visits Dr. Gettleman's office. 'He's behind the elephant' delivered with casual confidence implies he's found Waldo in that book many times before. Layers of implication packed into a brief exchange.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: I just told a joke about my parole officer and nobody laughed. Guess I'm better at breaking the law than breaking the ice.

jokes.text: So no ring. Can I assume you're also a single parent?
jokes.setup: Ross is hitting on a woman in the pediatrician's waiting room.
jokes.punchline: Ross's pickup line in the pediatrician's office is to bond over being 'single parents' — not realizing (or ignoring) the inherent contradiction of an adult man being a patient at a children's doctor while also trying to seem mature enough to date.
jokes.explanation: The attempted seduction is funny in context — Ross is clearly hoping she'll assume he's there for a child patient. The dramatic irony (the audience knows the truth) enriches the exchange.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: Well, I figured if I'm gonna be miserable anyway, I might as well help you guys out. Plus, I gotta say, watching you try to act natural was actually pretty entertaining.

jokes.text: Rossie? We're ready for you.
jokes.setup: Ross is mid-flirtation with an attractive single mother, presenting himself as a mature, capable single dad.
jokes.punchline: The nurse calls him by the childhood diminutive 'Rossie' — immediately exposing him as a regular adult patient at a pediatrician's office.
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode and one of the best of the season. The whole 'Ross still sees his pediatrician' thread has been perfectly constructed to culminate here. The name 'Rossie' does everything: it confirms the secret, destroys Ross's romantic pretension, and implies a long, comfortable pediatric history — all in one word. The structure of the buildup (Ross flirting, projecting maturity) makes the deflation maximally painful. Perfect economy, perfect timing, perfect character integration. Earns 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: I can't prove I play piano without a piano.

dialogue.speaker: Mary Ellen
dialogue.line: So prove it anyway.

jokes.text: Come on, Ross Jr. It's time to go in.
jokes.setup: Ross has just been called 'Rossie' by the nurse, blowing his cover.
jokes.punchline: In a desperate face-saving move, Ross addresses an invisible 'Ross Jr.' — implying there's a child he's supposedly there for — but there is no child and everyone knows it.
jokes.explanation: The topper to the best joke in the episode. Ross's desperate gambit of inventing a 'Ross Jr.' is both hilarious and deeply sad. The audience knows there's no child, the woman knows, and Ross knows she knows — and yet he commits. 'Come on, Ross Jr.' delivered to empty air is a classic sitcom image. Earns 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: Without a piano? Fine. *begins elaborate air piano performance with exaggerated hand movements and sound effects* Dun-dun-dun-dun! *dramatic flourish* There. Rachmaninoff.

jokes.text: Mommy, what's wrong with that man?
jokes.setup: Ross has just called out for 'Ross Jr.' in the pediatrician's waiting room.
jokes.punchline: A child in the waiting room asks her mother what's wrong with Ross — a final, crushing verdict on the whole sequence.
jokes.explanation: The perfect button on the pediatrician sequence. A child's innocent question — 'What's wrong with that man?' — is the cruelest possible assessment, delivered by the most innocent possible source. The irony of a child pitying the adult patient in a children's doctor's office is devastating. The room would erupt.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I play acoustic, folksy stuff.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, like heavy metal, but acoustic.

jokes.text: Hey, I helped you find Waldo!
jokes.setup: The child has just asked what's wrong with 'that man.' Ross is mortified.
jokes.punchline: His defensive response is to cite his Waldo assistance — implying he deserves credit (and perhaps pity) for his good deed.
jokes.explanation: The callback to the Waldo moment is perfect — Ross citing his only point of pride from the last five minutes as a character defense. 'Hey, I helped you find Waldo!' as a response to 'What's wrong with that man?' is a quotable, perfectly economical button. The gap between the accomplishment (finding Waldo) and what it's being used to defend (Ross's dignity) is the entire joke. Excellent craft.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.line: Wow, you're really good at finding Waldo. Does your son love those books?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Actually, I'm not that into them because of him. I've just always been really into them.

jokes.text: I got held up at Dr. Gettleman's office. There was some guy that freaked everybody out.
jokes.setup: Ross arrives late to say goodbye to Chandler; he explains his delay
jokes.punchline: He describes himself — the terrifying adult pediatric patient — as 'some guy' who 'freaked everybody out,' with no apparent self-awareness
jokes.explanation: Perfect button to the entire pediatrician arc. Ross describing himself as 'some guy who freaked everybody out' — with zero self-recognition — is a masterclass in oblivious character comedy. It's the best possible coda because it confirms Ross has no insight into how he appeared. This is as well-structured as a single-line callback can be. High character integration: only Ross could say this. Among the top jokes in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Hey buddy, it's me, Ross Jr.

jokes.text: Watch the tongue, people. We got a baby over here.
jokes.setup: Chandler and Monica share a passionate goodbye kiss before Chandler leaves for Tulsa.
jokes.punchline: Joey acts as an impromptu moral guardian on behalf of the baby — 'Watch the tongue, people' — a hilariously prudish directive from Joey of all characters.
jokes.explanation: Joey acting as a prude is excellent character irony — he is the last person who should be concerned about public displays of affection. 'Watch the tongue, people' is a great turn of phrase, and invoking the baby as justification elevates it. Character integration is strong.

dialogue.speaker: Child
dialogue.line: Mom, what's wrong with that man?

dialogue.speaker: Mother
dialogue.line: Nothing, honey.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I helped you carry your bags!

jokes.text: What's the matter, Joe? / I'm mad at you for leaving. You know, you're nothing but a big leaver. / A big leaver with a stupid suitcase.
jokes.setup: Joey is upset that Chandler is leaving for Tulsa.
jokes.punchline: His expression of hurt feelings is 'you're nothing but a big leaver' — an oddly specific, childlike construction — followed by 'with a stupid suitcase,' attacking the inanimate object.
jokes.explanation: 'Big leaver' and 'stupid suitcase' are written at exactly the right level of childlike pique — real hurt expressed through ridiculous vocabulary. Joey's emotional immaturity is on full display, and it's both funny and touching. 'Stupid suitcase' is the topper that sells it.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa! Hey! There's a baby in the room!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You guys, come on! She's gonna see this!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Do you want her to think that's how people say goodbye?

jokes.text: Any chance you're trying to pick a fight to make all of this easier? / [long pause] / Dude, you see right through me!
jokes.setup: Chandler calmly offers an insight into Joey's behavior — that he's manufacturing a fight to ease the goodbye.
jokes.punchline: After a pause (the beat of Joey being caught), he admits it with cheerful transparency: 'Dude, you see right through me!'
jokes.explanation: The pause before 'Dude, you see right through me!' is essential — Joey needs a moment to process the insight, then admits it with zero embarrassment. The lack of shame and the genuine admiration for Chandler's perception is a lovely character note. Good emotional depth with a funny button.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You know what? I am mad at you! You left me here!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Joey, I had to go to London for work.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh yeah? Well, you're... you're stupid! And your hair looks dumb! And that suitcase of yours is ugly and it smells!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Did you just insult my suitcase?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah! It's a stupid suitcase!

jokes.text: Can I talk now? / Okay, bye. / Joey! / He had to board.
jokes.setup: Everyone is saying heartfelt goodbyes to Chandler; Joey has been waiting to get a word in
jokes.punchline: By the time the emotional goodbyes end, Chandler has had to board — Joey never got to say his goodbye, which is both his comic due and genuinely a little sad
jokes.explanation: Sweet bittersweet button to the episode. Joey being denied his goodbye because the others took too long is both funny (his complaint is petty) and a little poignant (he was the most upset about Chandler leaving). Works as an episode closer but isn't a particularly crafted joke.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Are you picking a fight to make leaving easier?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah.

tmdb_overview: Rachel's pediatrician drops her as a client because she calls him incessantly to ask about any insignificant issue concerning Emma, so now she must find a new one, which puts Ross in an awkward situation. Meanwhile, Joey arranges a blind date for Phoebe. Also, as Chandler and Monica are preparing to leave for Tulsa, Monica receives a job offer from a prestige restaurant in Manhattan.
insight: Escalation-driven episode relies on character comedy cringe but never quite lands the big laugh.
